claims.text: Replacing laser- or electron-beam additive manufacturing with cold spray will minimize thermal input for AlCrFeNiSi feedstock.
The reduced thermal input from cold spray will reduce residual thermal stresses.
Cold spray will preserve the feedstock microstructure and thereby enhance mechanical properties.
Cold spray will simplify processing relative to conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
Cold spray can form AlCrFeNiSi parts through high-velocity particle impact without melting.
A substrate temperature below 100 degrees Celsius is an applicable processing condition for the proposed AlCrFeNiSi cold-spray process.
The process can be carried out in either ambient or inert atmosphere for miniature components with dimensions of a few millimeters.
Cold spray will retain the original fine-grained and potentially multiphase microstructure of the powder.
Interparticle bonding in cold-sprayed AlCrFeNiSi will be achieved by severe plastic deformation during impact.
Avoiding melting will prevent melting-induced grain growth and phase transformations.
Bypassing melt-solidification cycles will mitigate thermal gradients and associated residual stresses.
Cold spray will maintain the original microstructure and mechanical integrity of the AlCrFeNiSi feedstock.
Cold-sprayed components will have significantly lower residual thermal stresses than laser-powder-bed-fused or electron-beam-melted components.
Cold-sprayed components will have higher yield strength and ductility than components made by conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
Cold-sprayed components will require less complex post-processing than conventional high-thermal-load additively manufactured components.
Conventional laser powder bed fusion or electron beam melting of AlCrFeNiSi typically produces high residual stresses.
Conventional high-thermal-load processing of AlCrFeNiSi causes microstructural degradation through excessive thermal cycling.

The intervention is expected to be most effective for miniature AlCrFeNiSi components and may not transfer to larger structures or alloys with substantially different melting and solidification behavior.
Qualitative benefits from reducing thermal input through cold spray are already known.
The quantitative stress reduction, bonding strength, mechanical performance, and optimal particle-velocity and substrate-temperature window for AlCrFeNiSi remain undetermined.
